title: Python decorator workshops
description: Guided JupyterLab workshops that teach Python decorators: what they do, how to write them, and why they work. Standard library only, and they run in the browser.

workshops.name: what-a-decorator-does
workshops.title: What a decorator does
workshops.description: Meet decorators as a user before writing one. Put three decorators from the standard library to work, watch each change what a function or a class does, and find out what the @ line actually means.

workshops.name: your-first-decorator
workshops.title: Your first decorator
workshops.description: Write the thing that goes after the @. Wrap a function by hand, then with the @ syntax, then build a timer, a call counter, and decorators that act before, after and instead of the function they wrap.

workshops.name: how-a-decorator-remembers
workshops.title: How a decorator remembers
workshops.description: Find out how a wrapper still knows the function it wraps after the decorator has returned. Open a closure and look inside it, build functions that make functions, keep state with nonlocal, and meet the pitfall that catches everyone once.

workshops.name: decorators-that-take-arguments
workshops.title: Decorators that take arguments
workshops.description: Make a decorator work on any function, then make it configurable. Forward arguments with *args and **kwargs, add the extra layer that @repeat(3) needs, build a retry worth keeping, and handle a decorator used with and without parentheses.

workshops.name: preserving-the-wrapped-function
workshops.title: Preserving the wrapped function
workshops.description: Find out what a wrapper costs you, then fix it with one line. See what functools.wraps copies, why inspect still finds the original signature, and what is genuinely left over.

workshops.name: stacking-decorators
workshops.title: Stacking decorators
workshops.description: Put more than one decorator on a function and find out that they are applied in one order and run in another. See a stack where the order changes the answer, and walk the chain back to the original function.

workshops.name: decorating-methods
workshops.title: Decorating methods
workshops.description: Put a decorator on a method and meet the most common surprise in Python decorators. See which kinds work, find the instance hiding in args, write a decorator that uses it, and learn the real rule for stacking with staticmethod and classmethod.

workshops.name: class-based-decorators
workshops.title: Decorators that are classes
workshops.description: Write a decorator as a class rather than a function. Keep state in an instance attribute, restore the identity it quietly replaces, use the constructor in place of the extra layer a configurable decorator needs, and see what it still cannot do.

workshops.name: how-methods-bind
workshops.title: How methods bind
workshops.description: Find out how `obj.method()` finds its instance, by doing the binding by hand. Then fix the class-based decorator that could not do it, give a class its own `__get__`, and see that the protocol behind all of it is a plain language feature you can use directly.

workshops.name: decorating-classes
workshops.title: Decorating classes
workshops.description: Put a decorator on a class rather than a function. Synthesise a `__repr__`, add comparison and meet the hashing trap that comes with it, freeze a class against assignment, and find out that `@dataclass` is an ordinary decorator doing exactly what you have just done by hand.

workshops.name: caching-results
workshops.title: Caching results
workshops.description: Build the decorator you met in the first workshop. Write a naive cache, break it twice, fix the key with signature.bind, then use the standard library's own and find out what unbounded caching costs.

workshops.name: registering-functions
workshops.title: Registering functions
workshops.description: Write a decorator that wraps nothing and changes nothing. Build a command registry, a route table and an event system, and recognise the shape you have already used in Flask, Click and pytest.

workshops.name: retrying-and-handling-errors
workshops.title: Retrying and handling errors
workshops.description: Decorate the error path. Log a failure without swallowing it, translate an exception while keeping its cause, retry only the failures worth retrying, and watch the stacking order decide what ends up in your logs.

workshops.name: decorating-async-functions
workshops.title: Decorating async functions
workshops.description: Put an ordinary decorator on an async def and watch it fail without saying so. Write a wrapper that awaits, one decorator that serves both kinds, and find out what happens when a wrapper blocks the event loop.
